utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We will have the first witness, and for that purpose can we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please state your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: My name is Philip Coo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I'm working at the Special Tribunal for Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Coo, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I was employed for ten months at the UN International Independent Investigation Commission in Beirut and prior to that spent nine years at the ICTY working for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your current position, what's your job title, what do you do?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I'm now the head of analysis in the Office of the Prosecution -- Office of the Prosecutor at the Special Tribunal for Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during your time here at the ICTY in the OTP, what was your job?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I began in 1999 as an analyst in the military analysis team and retained that function throughout the nine years here, but in 2004 I added the function of head of the military analysis team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did you serve as the head of what we call MAT, M-A-T?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I was the -- I was the acting head until from -- I think it was August 2004 and was appointed formally in January 2005 and remained the head until I left in -- at the end of February 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what your background was in terms of education and experience that led you to performing that kind of work at the OTP.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I did a university degree in psychology and immediately after university in Canada I joined the Canadian Forces and became an army intelligence officer. I spent nine years as an army intelligence officer in a variety of functions from the tactical level to the strategic level at the national defence headquarters including one tour in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during your service at the OTP, did you work on any cases involving the conflict in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, all the cases I worked on were the Kosovo cases. I began by working on the Milosevic case, the Kosovo portion of that, and worked on that throughout the Milosevic trial and moved on to the Milutinovic case with a short period of time assisting on the Limaj case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the course of that work, did you write any reports that were tendered as expert reports in any of those cases?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Two of the reports I wrote were tendered as expert reports, the Milosevic report and the Limaj report. The report that I wrote for the Milutinovic case was an expert -- written on the basis of an expert report, and tendered, I believe, in the legal -- my understanding of the legal term is correct as an expert report, but I didn't testify as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you testify as an expert in any other cases?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I testified as an expert in Milosevic and in the Limaj cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we bring up 65 ter number 02845, please. And if the usher would assist me, I can hand a partial hard copy of this document to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is, Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report that I was asked by the Prosecution in the Milutinovic case to draft to account for the provenance of the materials that were used in the report that I had written for that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think the first five pages, four or five pages, are text describing how these documents used in your expert report were obtained; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And attached to it then was a list of all of the documents that had been used in your report, which up to that time, I think in February 2007, had not otherwise been admitted during the trial in the Milutinovic case?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would indicate for our purposes this document has that list of exhibits, I think it's 20 some pages. Many of those either were not on the 65 ter list in this case. Many of them have already been admitted in this case with another number. So we may later want to adjust this exhibit in e-court and perhaps remove that list to avoid any confusion, because I have an updated list which we now have in the system as 65 ter number 02845.01, which I've tried to bring up-to-date by removing from the list that's a part of this exhibit any that either are not being tendered in this trial or which have already been admitted with separate exhibit numbers, different from those that they had in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you're telling us what might happen in the future. We will await events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Coo, I want to go through with you the new list which I'll show you a little later. I think we've reduced it to now something like 95 or 96 exhibits. I don't intend to show you each and every one, but I want to pick some that are representative of various categories and then we'll talk about those shortly. But first I want to show you a couple documents that aren't on that list but I think you can help us with. And the first one is 02615.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Your Honour, I would like to tender 02845 at this time because I want you to have his text of that provenance report about how the documents were gathered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not presently being displayed. It's a very lengthy list I take it. I'm trying to identify --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- wishing to tender, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm just trying to tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it a document that has been put in our hands this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, it's not that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not that, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But it's a -- it's a five-page or four-page written report with a list attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, and it's not a document that's been previously used?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that my learned colleague has been talking about what he wants to have tendered, I would just like to say in advance that the Defence will not challenge or object to the admission of this document but without any attachments, so just the basic document, where it says what the origin was, how they came by the documents. As to the attachments, we're going to have some objections to some maybe. So that's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. This document will be received, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, I would indicate that those pages are ERNs K053-8187 up to and including 8191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, is it a document that we're likely to be referring to constantly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's just a background, resource document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 02845 will be Exhibit P01284.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll discuss that matter with the Registry Officer during the break about how we can perhaps clean that up and remove the old list of documents that is not pertinent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Coo, I wanted you to look at 02615. There are two pages, both maps. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That's a depiction of the information derived from a number of Joint Command orders covering the period mentioned on the graphic, the 23rd of March to the 4th of April. I had taken the geographical information from the Joint Command orders, which described where combat operations would take place as ordered by those particular orders. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you there, Mr. Coo, to hear what it is that Mr. Djordjevic wishes to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly understand, Your Honours, the will to the Prosecution to have this document tendered, but I'd like to remind my colleague that this Trial Chamber has decided that this witness here today can only be a witness to the facts, whereas we're now going into an expert opinion based on an analysis of the documents received. And I think the decision made was that something like that will not be possible when it -- we're dealing with Mr. Philip Coo, this gentleman here. So if -- in my view, this represents an expert report so it cannot be the subject of an examination-in-chief and even less so can it be tendered into evidence and admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I intend to ask the witness to explain how this was composed. At the end of that or later on, after we've talked about perhaps some of the Joint Command orders that underlie the composition of this map, I may move to tender it. I don't think that it's necessarily expert testimony, what's been done here. And I would indicate for Your Honours that in the Milutinovic case Mr. Coo was proposed as an expert. Judge Bonomy determined that given -- partly given the fact that he had participated in suspect interviews of some of the accused, interviews of numerous witnesses in the case, and because he was employed by our office, he was in essence too close to the Prosecution to be called as an expert, although he left it open whether or not his report could be an expert report, which was discussed during the trial. Two or three attempts were made to modify it to remove opinion. In the end it was not allowed, but he was allowed to testify, not as an expert but what in my jurisdiction we would call a summary witness. Someone in-house who had become familiar with a large collection of documents, organised them, understood them in a certain way, that could be helpful to the trier of fact. I don't know what it is in your various jurisdictions, Your Honours, but that's somebody who falls short of an expert but is somebody other than simply a fact witness, in terms of a percipient witness of the events at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I observe for the benefit of both counsel that this Chamber has indicated it will hear Mr. Coo as a witness of fact, not receive his report as an expert report. Now, that does not exclude that he may have knowledge and expertise which could ground opinion which we will receive; but what we have done because of Mr. Coo's closeness to and association with the Prosecution case is insisted that he be called and his evidence given orally so that, A, there is opportunity to deal with any aspect of it which is particularly affected by that closeness; and B, if it is that he moves into an area of opinion in some respect, that can be the subject of full cross-examination as needed. I am not familiar with what you call a summary witness, Mr. Hannis. This is a witness called as a witness of fact, but he may also be an expert for some purposes. What is important is that his evidence is not simply received by way of a written report. You have to deal with his evidence piece by piece, and if there is an area of expertise identified and he's adequately qualified, it may be that in that respect the Chamber will receive an opinion from the witness. Now, I hope that assists both counsel. We are very conscious of the fact that Mr. Coo has been very close to the Prosecution case, and we'll be evaluating whatever it is that he says in his evidence in light of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Djordjevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. All I wanted to do was to refer to your ruling of the 5th of March, 2009, especially points 19 and 20, from which I was able to conclude that this witness can only address the facts linked to how the documents were procured. And because of this close link with the OTP which has been going on, especially with respect to his work on the Kosovo cases, related cases, the Limaj case, the Milosevic and Milutinovic cases, this witness then in view of that -- well, his opinion and views can always be challenged because he has this close relationship with the OTP. On the other hand, I think that when we're dealing with things of this nature and when we have a document to decide upon, a document which the Defence deems goes beyond testimony about the facts - and as we've just heard from the witness, he compiled this map and marked the map - so this is a problem as far as the Defence is concerned with respect to the rights of the accused when it comes to witnesses of this kind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Djordjevic. I've been able to refresh my memory of paragraphs 19 and 20. I can understand that the position in which Mr. Coo stands may be not altogether clear to you. We are receiving him as a witness of fact. He may qualify on a particular matter as an expert, and we will receive his opinion if that should arise from his oral evidence. We are, though, very conscious of the question of his partiality of impartiality because of his association, and will therefore be evaluating what he says, including any opinion that he may be allowed to give in light of that circumstance. So it is not the fact that he may not be allowed to give any opinion whatever about matters, but we are wanting to hear him orally as a lay witness so that we can make a proper evaluation and so that you will have a full opportunity to cross-examine. We are not simply receiving a written expert report for the reasons that have been indicated. I hope that will assist you to understand what you have been reading. Now your concern with this document is that it is based on his reading or assessment of certain other documents. Now, we could debate for a day or two, conduct a seminar, on whether that involves expertise as an expert witness or it is merely the evaluation of factual material in the course of evidence. The Chamber, where it knows what it is that the witness has relied on to produce this, will usually be prepared to receive something like this as merely his assessment of the effect of some other documents presented in a convenient form. The Chamber will then assess that evidence as lay evidence to determine whether it agrees or does not agree with what the witness says about that matter and the views that he has reached. The -- in a sense, the special standing often accorded to an expert opinion is not going to sit upon the evidence of this witness, but that doesn't mean that he may not be able to express certain things. If he does, we will evaluate them for ourselves fully, not with the enhancement that might be given to his evidence if he were an expert but merely as a lay witness. So if you could continue, Mr. Hannis. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just be allowed to say something briefly. I'm just wondering whether we are experts enough to be able to evaluate his opinions and his conclusions linked to documents of this type. Nothing more than that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will do our best. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, could you explain for us how you went about preparing this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to pause between questions and answers for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- we had a -- I reviewed a series of Joint Command orders, ordering combat operations, and those orders specified where the operations should occur by referring to geographical features. For the most part, those features were towns and villages. I plotted those features on a map of Kosovo and -- by hand and then asked an assistant in trial support, Iain Reid, to convert the hand-drawn maps to an electronic form. And the electronic form is this exhibit which I had checked once Iain Reid had drawn the electronic form, I confirmed that it was -- matched the form that I drew.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on your experience in working on investigations and indictments arising out of incidents in Kosovo, is this an accurate graphic depiction of the shape of Kosovo and the various locations of the towns and, I guess, Dubrava prison named thereon?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I believe it is, Your Honours. I can't recall precisely where I -- I got the map from, but it was an official map, if my memory serves me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you make these graphic representations where you've drawn various shapes in colour at certain locations? For example, the green shape which we see in your list refers to a Joint Command order dated the 23rd of March - with an ERN of K052-5806. What did you do with that Joint Command order to be able to draw that shape?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I took from the section of that Joint Command order which described by reference to the geographical features where the future combat operations as ordered in the order would take place, and I copied those on to a map of Kosovo. And the area bounded by these geographical features was, from my interpretation of the Joint Command order, where these future combat operations were to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on your work and your participation in the Kosovo cases and your testimony in various trials related to Kosovo, were you aware of whether or not the operations set forth in those Joint Command orders actually took place, do you know?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: My understanding was that the operations did take place and conformed generally to the way in which they were ordered in the Joint Command orders, and I came to that assessment by reviewing a document such as daily combat reports and war diaries where the units that were taking part in the combat operations were reporting on their activities to their superior headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Djordjevic has arisen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just briefly, let me refer to this witness's testimony, who says that in electronic form he introduced this information -- that this information was introduced by Iain Reid, as he said, and it was a case manager -- he was a case manager in the pre-trial proceedings of this trial. So that is yet another reason for my objecting. So he was a case manager in the pre-trial of this case, the person who was related to this map and this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, is it the position that the depiction on the map in front of you is one which in your assessment reflects the effect of the orders that you have referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. I -- once Mr. Reid had transcribed my hand-drawn depiction in electronic form, I confirmed it against the hand-drawn depiction and the Joint Command orders and considered that the electronic depiction was accurate. So I took responsibility for the accuracy of these graphics, not Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it then a correct understanding that the work of Mr. Reid was undertaken because of his school with electronic presentation rather than his evaluation of the original documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's the sole reason why he was involved in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For that reason, Mr. Djordjevic, we would not accept the validity of your objection. Mr. Reid is in the capacity of an electronic draftsman in drawing rather than in any way making any -- himself any evaluation of the source material on the evidence that was made by this witness. Carry on, please, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we go to page 2 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My understanding, Mr. Coo, is that by that description that first map that we looked at covered the time-period from 23 March to 24 April 1999?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And now the second map we have here, was this created in the same fashion you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see on the document itself it says it's for operations conducted during the period of mid-April to May 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I have no more questions about that at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document. I would indicate for your benefit and counsel's benefit that some of the Joint Command orders listed here, I think some may already be in evidence but most of them are not yet in evidence. So if you prefer I wait until I've addressed some of those additional Joint Command orders, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be tendering them all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe they're all on my list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber would receive the tendered maps. It would do so subject to Mr. Djordjevic's objection, which we note but we have overruled. It does so on the simple factual basis, Mr. Hannis, that if you don't in the end prove the source material, we're not going to be able to place any reliance at all on this visual presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So it's up to you to make good the foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not my intention to comment further. I have stated my objections. But as to the way in which documents are to be admitted and tendered, I think it would be more useful and we'd save more time if my learned friend would do this step by step as his alternative, as a second possibility, because then the Defence would have quite a number of objections to make. First of all, as you said, Mr. President, the authenticity of the documentation, to begin with, that can of course be dealt with during the cross-examination. But I think we'll save more time as we take each document in turn, as was Mr. Hannis's second alternative. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you have any submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could go now to the updated list of the documents in Mr. Coo's provenance report and address some of the Joint Command orders that are on that list and underline this map. I could do that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But is that going to advance the coherent presentation of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's my eternal hope with whatever I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber I think, Mr. Hannis, is of the view that it would stay with what has been indicated. Can I once more try and quickly explain the Chamber's approach to these matters for the assistance of counsel. When the establishment of facts involves a number of steps such as here, the witness is saying, I've looked at a number of Joint Command orders. In my view they indicate certain things which can be depicted on a map. That has been done, in this case it's been done electronically, it looks better, and it's easier to follow. In the end, that represents my understanding of what certain orders say. Now, that's one set of factual issues. It's an aid to everybody in the courtroom understanding the evidence and understanding of the witness. If it is the case that some of the documents relied on by the witness are in the end not admitted into evidence or if they're admitted into evidence in the end the Chamber concludes that it can't accept them as genuine or it concludes that its understanding of the document is different from the witness's, well then this map ceases to have its force and validity. It's in evidence, but our own evaluation as a Chamber tells us we can't rely on what is being shown in it. We've got to start somewhere at understanding the history of events, and in that process a map of this nature may well be of assistance. So we start at a logical place. There are other logical ways of dealing with all the evidence, but in the end, wherever we start, there have to be certain factual decisions made. For instance, if we started the other way and wanted to have all the basic documents first proved, we may not be in a position to evaluate whether they are genuine or not, whether we accept them or not at this stage of the trial. We may have to wait to the end of the trial before being able to reach a final decision. Now, it's not the case that we must reach a final decision about those matters now before we can move on to evidence of this nature. It will just have to be understood that we will hear and evaluate objections as to the genuineness, the reliability, and the true interpretation and any other point that's raised of these various sorts of documents by the time we come to make a final evaluation of the whole case. That having been done, we start with this depiction of what this witness considers those documents reveal as an easy way into understanding other parts of his evidence. And we will be dealing with objections that are made as they arise and we may have to reserve our decision about them, but at the end of the day this evidence and this map or these maps will have no more force than we are able to make of the reliability of the source documents relied on to produce these maps and of the proper interpretation of those source documents. So it's not that the Defence is going to lose any advantage whatever, however we approach this task; in the end the final evaluation will have to be made by the Chamber on the basis of all the evidence about these matters. Now, I've spent some time in two or three occasions so far in trying to explain our position to assist counsel to understand. I don't want to have to keep doing that. We have noted the objections of Mr. Djordjevic. They'll be taken into account. They'll be evaluated in the course of the other evidence, including and especially of his cross-examination of this and other witnesses about those source documents before we come to a final decision. So I will now ask you to continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go back to the first map I can give some indication regarding those Joint Command orders which -- regarding the first map, all of those appear to be in evidence in this case already, and I can indicate the numbers for which ones perhaps we can take note of now. The first Joint Command order that's represented by the colour green is Exhibit P972 in evidence. For the blue it's Exhibit D105. For the red, Exhibit P350. The purple, Exhibit P371. For the orange, Exhibit P970. And lastly, at the bottom, for the yellow, P1235. And Ms. Kravetz is assisting me in double-checking the ones on the second page. But with that in mind, Your Honour, I would ask to tender this map at this time and any -- I know there are a few Joint Command orders regarding the second map that are not yet in evidence, but they are on the list that I intend to go through with Mr. Coo today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first map will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01285.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you proceed also to tender the second at this stage, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to, Your Honour. I can preliminarily indicate that a couple of Joint Command orders regarding that second page in this exhibit, the map for mid-April to May 1999 are already in evidence. The second one for -- with a start date of 15 April 1999 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, we haven't got the map on the screen yet, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will help us if it comes up as you speak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now on this map, the second one, K052-0059 that's in evidence as P766. And then going down to the last two, start date of 23 April K052-0089 and P767, and the last one in green K052-0084 on 25 April is P969.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Now that map also will be received subject to the same objections and on the basis that I have sought to amplify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I would like to turn to what's in e-court as 65 ter number 0284501 -- point 01.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the second map will be Exhibit P01286.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if the usher could assist me, I'd like to hand Mr. Coo a hard copy of this. And I would indicate, Your Honours, now I am going to be referring to the hard-copy document that was handed out to you and Defence counsel at the start of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, I would indicate to you, this is the reduced list from the original list that was attached to your provenance report. And I have removed from it those documents that either we, the Prosecution, decided not to tender in the Djordjevic case and those documents which were already received in this case and have an exhibit number in this case. So you'll see it's a somewhat smaller list than what you originally had attached to your provenance report. And you describe in the MAT comments column on the far right the source or how the particular documents were received. I want to ask you about some particular ones. And the first one I would like to show you is exhibit -- well, it's 65 ter number 00717. And on your hard copy that will be item number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, and Mr. Djordjevic, I would indicate that this document is in MOS exhibit number order from lowest to highest, so that may assist in following as I go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, do you recognise 00717 that's on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges where the OTP received this document and how?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't recall -- this is one of the few that I don't recall the provenance of. It was already in our system when I was preparing my report. I came across it through electronic searches of our system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on your experience in working on the case and testifying in the Milosevic and Milutinovic cases -- well, did you also follow those trials that you were a participant in?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I followed those trials closely, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you aware of this particular document being presented in both of those cases?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on that, do you have any information about authenticity of this particular exhibit?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I believe the contents of the letter from the former Chief of the General Staff, General Perisic, are accurate. They were assessed against other documentation that had been acquired independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you aware of discussions about this document in the Milosevic trial and the Milutinovic trial?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I was, Your Honours. I believe it -- there was a -- the contentious point was the allegation about the existence of a Joint Command and the illegal use of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of anything else outside the contents of the letter itself that would suggest what's written therein is accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I believe it's -- the authenticity is supported by the official stamp, the format of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to indicate once again that the Defence has understood it that this witness can be asked about what he knows, what knowledge he has, and not what he thinks. That's all from me. Thank you. The answers the witness has been giving is what he thinks and not what he knows. So may we stick to the facts and hear what he knows and what knowledge he has. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Fair comment, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would indicate that some of the witness's knowledge comes from following two trials in which this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And the simple issue is whether or not from its face and its earlier use this document can be accepted as reliable or not, as to which the Chamber is not in a position to make a final judgement at this time. And so it will be assessed for that question as well as what use is made of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Let me move to Exhibit P -- I'm sorry, 65 ter number 01000, 01000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, do you recognise the document that's on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is and how OTP came into possession of this one?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The document is the minutes of the body called the Supreme Defence Council, which was comprised of the president of Yugoslavia and the presidents of the member states, and included the Chief of the General Staff in most of the meetings. The document, I believe, was acquired by -- in response to a request for assistance to the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or its successors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a general question to this point. Requests for assistance, sometimes referred to by the acronym RFAs, can you explain briefly to the Judges what that process is and how it works in the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: When the OTP felt that a particular category of information or a particular document likely existed in the archives or the holdings of a state or information, whether documentary or not, we would draft a request for assistance addressed to that state requesting the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to Serbia in particular, do you know how documents were processed once they were drafted in the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who -- first of all, who signs them in the OTP when they're sent out to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: They were signed by the Prosecutor and then sent through the Serbian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which would ensure that the -- the request was sent to the proper bodies within Serbia itself who could provide the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know how it worked on the Serbian end? Was there a particular entity or person who was responsible for dealing with the RFAs from the OTP, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't know of a particular individual, but there was a -- on the VJ requests that were requesting VJ documentation there was a VJ commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to a document like this, the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council, would that go to a different entity or the same, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: There was an entity, but the name of it escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It was responsible for coordinating the responses to requests for assistance from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when these RFAs were responded to, what form did that take? What did the OTP get back, based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: If we had requested that documents and the response was successful, normally we would get back a covering letter attached to which were the documents that we had requested, or the letter would indicate that these documents would follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to this particular exhibit which is a session of the SDC on 25 December 1998, are you familiar with the contents of this meeting or the minutes of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would indicate, you'll see on the document there is a list of these documents, items number 44 through 47 on your list which have the MOS exhibit numbers P01574 through 1577 are similar documents, they're minutes of other sessions of the SDC, the 5th, 6th, 7th, and 9th sessions. You'll see from the MAT comment that these also were received in response to an RFA, the same number as the one that pertains to 01000 on the screen now. So I bring that to your attention because they're from the same source on the same date and they're the same kind of document. I don't know what the best procedure, Your Honour, is, if I should try to introduce these now. I had proposed to talk about some of the different categories on the list, and then I wanted to tender all the documents on Mr. Coo's list, but it may be more appropriate to deal with them one at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How many do you need to deal with specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to these five I have one, two, three, four -- I have another 12, and one of those contains about six documents, it's Joint Command orders. So I'll treat that group of six as a block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber thinks it might avoid potential confusion or difficulty by dealing with each of the ones that are subject to particular comment as they are dealt with. In that regard with respect to item number 3 and in respect of item number 7, the two you have dealt with, the Chamber is prepared to receive as -- and accept the admissibility of each of those I think categories rather than particular documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It does so on the basis that it will need to make a final evaluation, and that if in its final evaluation it is not satisfied, well then those documents will not be accorded weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would ask then in conjunction with 01000 that you treat similarly 01574, 01575, 01576, and 01577 similarly, as they all come from the same source, the same date, in response to the same request for assistance, and they are all minutes of Supreme Defence Council sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We do so on the basis that on the face of these documents there is a sufficient basis of apparent reliability to justify them being received, but we'll re-evaluate that issue if there is other evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- or other bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I request, I guess -- I don't think I need to, but may I request that at the end of the day if there are some of these or all of these that you find not sufficiently reached the mark for you that the Prosecution be permitted to make a written filing in the form of a bar table motion either addressing concerns regarding authenticity or relevancy or probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would certainly be practical if there is particular objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- which is pursued on some evidentiary basis. But in respect of some of these documents, we may hear no more about them until we come to make our final decision, in which event our silence will need to be taken as our confirmation of the view we've tentatively expressed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, are you proposing that these be admitted separately or simply the whole 97?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're going to spend a couple of days, I fear, just sorting out this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I would not want to make all of us sit through that, but I think each of the documents that has a separate exhibit number here probably needs a separate exhibit number in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we might deal with that then, as it were, on -- by a motion en masse at the end of this document and it can be sorted out administratively rather than proceed document by document orally here, which will take a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Your Honour. I think that's what I'll try to do. I'll address some of the ones that I particularly want to bring your attention to. I'm sure my learned friend across the hall will raise objections about any that he particularly has difficulty with. And at the end of the day then I'll be able to make such a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Right. Proceed down your particular path, Mr. Hannis, for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter number 01011. And, Your Honour, if I may, I would indicate that Mr. Coo, if it assists him, I would suggest that he may look at his hard copy of the list if he needs to to refresh his memory about the provenance of a particular document as long as he indicates on the record that he's doing that instead of from the top of his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, which particular document is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be the one that's number 8 on your hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Number 8, yes. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to object straight away to having this document admitted and the documents that emanate from this one, because I think that the level of reliability cannot be such as to be considered absolutely correct and that everything in this book is correct and reliable, but I'll deal with that during the cross-examination. On the other hand, I will make a submission on what the Defence is not going to agree upon. There is certain matters, as we're dealing with administrative matters, that were dealt with at Status Conferences. For example, the provision on the Ministry of the Interior and its organisation. The Prosecution and Defence have agreed on which one is valid, whereas here I see the law that we jointly agreed was not relevant and not applicable during a particular period of time. But not to waste any time, the Defence, too, would like to be as efficient as possible in these proceedings, and we're going to prepare a submission and we'll provide it to the Prosecution and of course the Trial Chamber, with your permission, in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Grateful indeed for that, Mr. Djordjevic, but can you just help me with this document. Are you saying that you object that some of the contents of the document are not reliable or are you saying this isn't what it purports to be, a document of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally have no knowledge about that, but I see that this is a book, a publication compiled by a certain Ivan Markovic. Now, I don't know the weight that this author has. I don't know who the author is, what material he used, and did he use authentic material in compiling this book. Now, as to who published this book, as for the time being I cannot state my views about that. So that's why I said that we will be making a submission on matters of this kind. Because what the expert referred to then and he's a witness here now was certain documentation and assertions which were -- are allegedly documented in this particular book. But there was a proper way to clear up whether this document was authentic or not in collecting the documents from the archives of the Army of Yugoslav and a request to give assistance by the body that we heard existed in Serbia in charge of cooperation with The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I can try to address some of that with the witness, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, where did this document come from? How did the OTP get it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: We came across a reference to it on the VJ's web site and had some -- someone from our field office in Belgrade go to a shop which we -- I know is the VJ bookshop to buy a copy of this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we could go to page 3 in e-court, page 3 of this document in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see that on your screen, Mr. Coo, do you see Press and Information Centre, Vojska?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what that is or was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Vojska is the publishing house --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: -- the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you seen the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I've read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And some of the -- well, what kind of documents does it contain?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The book refers in a number of areas to orders issued by the VJ, and they include excerpts or pictures of those orders, the -- purported to be the original orders. Some of those orders we did come across during our archive missions or documents provided in responses to RFAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the documents that you found during searches and received pursuant to RFAs that are -- that copies of are contained in this book, are they the same? Do they appear to be the same?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The ones that I was concerned with in drafting my report I did find to be the same. We didn't attempt to verify every single order in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you found none that were not consistent with the ones that you had gathered yourselves, either pursuant to RFAs or pursuant to searches?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to ask about that one, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would now like to look at 01259. This is number 29 on your hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, this purports to be a document from the Federal Ministry of Defence, Pristina defence administration. Do you recall where you got this one?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't recall this specifically. There's so many orders that we got from a variety of means, RFAs, archive missions, collected in Kosovo. I'd have to check the document just to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we look at page 2. I'm sorry, I need to go to the last page, the signature page. I see Mr. Djordjevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd like to request that we clear up the question of the authenticity of the document first, since I see that the source, the provenance, is a member of the Prosecution team, Mr. Fred Abrahams, that's number one. And number two is: I see that another source is Mr. Ylber Hysa. So as to the authenticity of this document, well that is questionable. So let's clear that up first; see what this is about. And the same refers to the document -- the three documents listed above, but we'll deal with that in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The course we are now following is that the Prosecution will identify documents that it feels require specific assistance from the evidence of the witness. You, as I understand it, wish to make a written submission in objection. And when we've finished this process, we'll identify a time by which that will be done and we will then make a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's better. Now I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who Petar Ilic was from other documents that you may have looked at in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours. He was in charge of a Ministry of Defence -- a Federal Ministry of Defence body in Kosovo which was responsible for a function known as civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think you indicated in your comments concerning this document that the authenticity is supported by official stamps?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. In assessing the authenticity of this, I would look at the -- for the existence of official stamps, for a signature block, reference number, assess the contents to see whether they're corroborated by documents gained independently. And in addition, if my memory serves me correctly, I don't believe there was anything inciteful - that's inciteful with a C - in this document that would warrant anyone going to the effort of forging before giving it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your comment also indicated that there was corroboration of the general concept of local security in Kosovo shown by other independently acquired documents. Do you recall what you were referring to there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes. There was a concept which I'd referred to as local defence in Kosovo, where they had set up village defence forces in non-Albanian villages and involved a mixture of -- or various organisations were involved, the VJ, the MUP, and it involved the arming of local civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, I would indicate or I would refer you to the testimony of General Djakovic, when he was here we showed him some documents signed by Mr. Ilic concerning Joint Command instructions for the defence of populated areas. That, I think, pertains to this remark. And I don't recall the exhibit numbers in this case. I know they were 65 ter numbers I think 01064 and 01067, but I'm not up to speed on the exhibit number in this case. If we could go next to 01268. While that's coming up, Your Honours, may I inquire when we should break. I know we were starting a little later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're close to the time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At a convenient break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me do this one, Your Honour, and then I will ask for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, do you recognise this document? It's dated the 30th of April, 1999, purportedly signed by General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And any comment on authenticity of this one?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It complied with another document that we had acquired through an RFA, which was the rules of correspondence and office administration in the VJ, where it set out how the correspondence in -- the format, among other things, to be used in various correspondence in the VJ is set out. This document has a stamp, a signature, and a signature block. It -- the content appears to be corroborated by other documents that I had reviewed, and generally it appears -- it has a reference number and generally appears to comply with the VJ's methods for drafting documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the content of this document dated 30 April 1999 in terms of relating to clearing of the battle-field, is that something that was a topic being discussed at that time in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps we could take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Hannis. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down, Mr. Coo. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Next I would like to look at 01318, that's number 32 on your hard copy, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, do you see that document? It appears to be a response from Serbia to an OTP RFA?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what -- the genesis of this, where this came from, how it came about?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: This was a response to, I think, our original request for documentation on the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would indicate -- Your Honours, I would remind the Court that when General Djakovic was here we tendered an exhibit with him concerning the Joint Command that was a response to an RFA. That was Prosecution Exhibit Number P1245.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us in your investigation in the MAT concerning Joint Command, how did you first learn about it? How did it first come up on your radar screen, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The -- there were references to a Joint Command in 1998 and some of the documents from that year. For example, there was a document on the defence of populated places in Kosovo which was issued under the authority of something called the Joint Command. So this piqued our interest, and I believe early on another witness, a VJ officer, had told us that he had attended a Joint Command meeting in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your initial request for documents from Serbia, what did they indicate about the existence of a Joint Command in 1999, initially?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The initial responses from -- at that time it was the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was that the Joint Command did not exist in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This document talks about -- it uses the term "shared command." Where does that come from and is that different from Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't know if that's -- I would presume that that's a translation issue. That's a response to a request from us about the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would indicate, Your Honours, perhaps we can engage the assistance of the interpreters but in the B/C/S copy on the left-hand side of the page the third line down in the main body I see what I seem to recognise from experience is "Zajednicka Komanda" which generally has been interpreted as Joint Command in the other documents I'm familiar with. I don't know if we can inquire from my learned friends across the way or from the interpreters whether I'm stating that correctly or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would invite any comment from the interpreter. We're getting no comment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Joint Command is indeed "Zajednicka Komanda."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Joint Command. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While we're understanding language, in your question that's just gone off the screen referred to the MAT, what on earth is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is our acronym for military analysis team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was a unit that Mr. Coo worked in. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after you got this response in November 2002, did you later learn of any information suggesting that there had been a Joint Command functioning and in existence in 1999 in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, we did. One of the -- the key things that allowed us to seek it with some authority was the -- we came across a reference in a -- I think in a VJ order, I think it was a Pristina Corps order or a General Staff order which referred to a Joint Command order of the 15th of April, 1999. So we then requested that Joint Command order by making reference to the reference number and the date and the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did that come up when General Delic testified in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: There was certainly a reference through General Delic's testimony, and in one of the Milosevic Defence witness exhibits which allowed us to make the request by referring to a very specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you see the signature block on this, it's the president of the commission, Lieutenant-General Terzic. Do you know what that commission was? I see at the top it says: "Commission for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal." What do you know about that body and General Terzic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't know much about General Terzic, other than what it says here about his title. I know the body was put together in the VJ to provide -- to act on requests for assistance from the OTP. So those requests would filter down through the -- from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs once they had left the ICTY and I -- in my opinion they would be then given to the VJ commission, and the VJ commission would then ensure or its role would be to acquire the documentation that we were asking for in theory and provide those documents to us and also to review those documents to he see if there were any, for example, national security interests that required protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who was instrumental in creating that VJ commission for cooperation?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It was General Pavkovic, who was Chief of the General Staff at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know who the members of the commission were or some of the members of the commission?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't. I believe that General Djakovic, who was a staff officer in the 3rd Army during 1999, was a member of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move on now to a document that is 65 ter number 01615. It's number 57 on your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's entitled an operations log or war log for the 3rd Army forward command post. When and how did OTP receive this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The OTP received this near the end of General Pavkovic's tenure as Chief of the General Staff. He -- the record in our files is that he handed a package of documents over to President Djindjic, and these were given to the Prosecutor at the time, Ms. Carla del Ponte.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you've reviewed the document itself for content?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And any remarks on authenticity?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I believed -- I didn't see any reason to believe why it wasn't authentic. The operations log or -- and war diary, it's called an operations log before a state of war and then a war diary for the period during the state of war. The contents of the operations log and the war diary tended to match the contents of documents acquired independently. And those documents included reports from subordinate units such as daily combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I'd like to see 65 ter 01878.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please switch off his microphone when not using it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about this one, Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, this is a Joint Command order that I've seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And any remarks you can make about authenticity of this particular Joint Command order?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Again, it corresponds to the document that I'd referred to earlier, which is the VJ rules on office correspondence or office administration and correspondence. It has a header, a serial number. It matches the format of a military order in terms of the subheadings, and the operations ordered in this Joint Command order were compared with documentation, daily operations reports, daily combat reports, war diaries of the subordinate units which were engaged in the operations that were ordered. And we could see that the subordinate units were, in fact, conducting operations which did correspond largely to the contents of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about the registry number at the top under Joint Command, that number 455-148, does that have any significance for you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The 455 series of orders was used for Joint Command orders, but in addition, 455 was used for Pristina Corps orders. And if I recall, 455-1 was a Pristina Corps order from, I think, January 1999 which covered combat operations in Kosovo, future combat operations in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would indicate for Your Honours, that's an exhibit in evidence already. I don't recall the number, but it was the 16th of February, 1999, signed by General Lazarevic, it's 455-1. Can we look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see there's no signature on this. Any comment about that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: The lack of a signature would be in contravention to the regulations and the rationale for issuing orders, and I had no explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that lack of signature common to all the Joint Command orders that you found from 1999?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It was with the exception of one Joint Command order, which was in fact an amendment to a Joint Command order, and that had the Pristina Corps commander's signature block on it and signature, General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, that's D105 in evidence, the document that the witness just referred to. All right. I would like now to move to 01878 -- or, I'm sorry, that's the one we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I had another question about this one. Do you recall seeing a document that was signed by General Ojdanic that was entitled "Suggestions"?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would indicate you have seen that too from when General Djakovic testified, it's Exhibit P1236 in evidence. Next I want to look at 01898.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That doesn't tell us much on the cover, but do you recognise that just from the cover page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is item number 61 on your list, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not from the cover page. Most of the time I was looking at the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, actually -- I think I see a reference to a Poetry Day, it must be the notebook of a MUP officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we're not getting to the meat of the matter. On your list you have this notebook listed as belonging to a particular person. Do you need to look at your list to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: No, I don't. It's the -- the notebook of General Obrad Stevanovic, a MUP officer, a member of the public security department of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when and how did this come to OTP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't remember the year. It was during the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember did --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I see Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I promised, I wouldn't be on my feet unless I considered this to be very important. The authenticity of this document can only be confirmed by the individual whom the witness just mentioned, that is to say General Obrad Stevanovic. Every other possibility is excluded, and that is why the Defence very fervently objects to these diaries, notebooks, or whatever they were called by the Prosecutor, and we feel that that is in contravention to the Rules of Procedure, especially so as this witness did not have any direct contact, as far as I know, with General Obrad Stevanovic. And everything he knows he knows -- is second-hand knowledge which, of course, has not been checked out and verified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you'll be including that again in your written submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, are you aware of General Stevanovic testifying during the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was this diary shown to him during the trial?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what comment, if any, did he make about whether it was his?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I -- I can't say for certain, but my memory of his testimony is that he essentially confirmed that this was his diary. He may have had some questions about particular parts of it, but largely it was a confirmation of it being his diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember him testifying about a particular meeting that is described in the diary, a particular meeting on or about the 20th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: There was testimony about a meeting concerning cleansing of the battle-field and crimes, investigation of crimes, in Kosovo, a high-level meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he confirm that part of the diary was written by him?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like to next show you 01905. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your spreadsheet indicates this was received in response to an RFA from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any comments on its apparent authenticity?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Again, it has the -- correspondence to the VJ's rules for drafting documentation, it has the required header, footer, security classification, and I don't see a signature but there may well be a signature and stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to next look at 01922.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This one has a couple of stamps and a signature. Do you recall what this one was about, where you got it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is number 65 on the list, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically whether we got this through an RFA or in an archive -- during an archive visit, but I believe it was one of those two means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know you indicated you don't remember presently where you got it, but on your spreadsheet there were indications about this coming pursuant to a response to an RFA. Are you comfortable that the entries on the spreadsheet regarding your comments are accurate?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see this document appears to be talking about the destruction of certain daily operations and combat reports from 1998, do you recall that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Djordjevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly. I think that leading questions are being asked here during the examination-in-chief which I don't consider to be fair. The witness can certainly answer because he has a hard copy of this list and once again we know who compiled the list. So I think what the witness said suffices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall -- do you recall this one, Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to determine whether or not that destruction was in the regular course of VJ business or do you know?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't know for certain. I know that there are regulations on the destruction of documentation and, for example, if combat reports, combat-related reports, produced during a state of war have to be retained permanently or for a much longer period than those produced outside the time of war. It sets out four specific categories of documentation, how long they are to be retained for in archives, and destruction has to be logged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at the last page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see the signer on this document is Lieutenant-General Susic. Do you know who he was, what position he held in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: He held the position on the Supreme Defence Council as the -- I think his title was the secretary of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He took the minutes of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And, Mr. Coo, are you familiar with a document -- the minutes of a meeting that was called the Inter-Departmental Staff for the Suppression of Terrorism in Kosovo that took place on the 29th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that document, I believe, also indicated that General Susic was the note-taker in that meeting, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically whether he was. I'd have to see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were there any other minutes or documents of meetings of that group other than that one from 29 October?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: To my recollection, that's the only one that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there -- was there other evidence to indicate that there had been other meetings besides that one?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like next to look at a series of Joint Command orders and the first one will be 01970. While that's coming up, Your Honours, I would indicate that in Exhibit P1286, which was the second map we showed earlier, I've noted there is a typographical error in the ERN and the date for one of those Joint Command orders. It's for the colour brown and K052-8502 should be K036-8502 and the date should be the 15th of April. What I propose to do is, with Mr. Reid's help, make a correction to that date and that ERN and substitute it if Mr. Djordjevic has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.
